description: An introduction to magnets and their poles, the law of magnetic poles, magnetic fields and materials, magnetization and demagnetization, electromagnets, and the everyday uses of magnetism.

mcq.questionText: A magnet is an object that:

options.text: Attracts magnetic materials such as iron, cobalt and nickel
Has no effect on any material

mcq.explanation: A magnet attracts iron, cobalt and nickel (and their alloys). Exam Tip: Not ALL materials are attracted - only magnetic ones. Wood, plastic, copper are not.

mcq.questionText: The two ends of a bar magnet, where the magnetic force is strongest, are called the:
mcq.explanation: These points are the poles (north and south). Exam Tip: Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole; force is weakest in the middle.

options.text: Have no effect on each other

mcq.explanation: Like poles push apart - they repel. Exam Tip: Like poles repel (N-N or S-S); unlike poles attract (N-S).
Unlike poles pull together - they attract. Exam Tip: Unlike poles attract (N-S); like poles repel.

mcq.questionText: The region around a magnet where its magnetic force can be detected is called the:
mcq.explanation: This region is the magnetic field. Exam Tip: Magnetic field lines can be shown using iron filings.

mcq.questionText: Magnetic field lines around a bar magnet run from:

options.text: South pole to north pole (outside the magnet)
North pole to south pole (outside the magnet)

mcq.explanation: Outside the magnet, field lines leave the north and enter the south. Exam Tip: Field lines go N to S outside, and S to N inside (closed loops).

mcq.questionText: Which of the following materials is magnetic?
mcq.explanation: Iron is attracted by a magnet. Exam Tip: Magnetic materials: iron, cobalt, nickel (and steel).

mcq.questionText: The process of making a magnetic material into a magnet is called:
mcq.explanation: Making something into a magnet is magnetization. Exam Tip: Magnetization methods: stroking with a magnet, or using electric current.

mcq.questionText: The process of removing the magnetism from a magnet is called:
mcq.explanation: Removing magnetism is demagnetization. Exam Tip: Demagnetization methods: hammering, heating strongly, or dropping repeatedly.

mcq.questionText: A soft iron bar can be magnetized by stroking it repeatedly, in the SAME direction, with one pole of a permanent magnet. This method is called:
mcq.explanation: Stroking with one pole, same direction is the single-stroke (touch) method. Exam Tip: Single-stroke: one pole, same direction, lifted away and returned to start each time.

mcq.questionText: Passing an electric current through a coil of wire wound around an iron core produces a(n):
mcq.explanation: Current + coil + iron core produces an electromagnet. Exam Tip: Electromagnets switch on/off with current - used in cranes, bells, relays.

mcq.questionText: Materials that keep their magnetism for a long time after being magnetized, such as steel, are called:
mcq.explanation: Materials that KEEP magnetism (steel) are hard/permanent magnetic materials. Exam Tip: Steel = hard, keeps magnetism. Soft iron = loses magnetism quickly.

mcq.questionText: Soft iron is preferred for making the core of an electromagnet because it:

options.text: Magnetizes and demagnetizes easily (loses magnetism quickly when current stops)

mcq.explanation: Soft iron magnetizes quickly with current and loses magnetism quickly when current stops. Exam Tip: Soft iron is ideal for electromagnets; steel is ideal for permanent magnets.

mcq.questionText: A simple test to find the north pole of an unmarked bar magnet is to:

options.text: Suspend it freely and see which end points towards geographic north

mcq.explanation: A freely suspended magnet aligns with Earth's field; the end pointing north is the north-seeking pole. Exam Tip: This is exactly how a magnetic compass works.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a practical use of magnets?

options.text: In a magnetic compass for direction-finding

mcq.explanation: Compasses use a magnetized needle to show direction. Exam Tip: Other uses: electric bells, cranes, electric motors, generators, loudspeakers.

fib.questionText: The ends of a magnet where the magnetic force is strongest are called ____.
fib.explanation: Every magnet has a north and a south pole, and the magnetic force is strongest at these ends. Exam Tip: Every magnet has a north and a south pole.

fib.questionText: Like poles of a magnet ____ each other.
fib.explanation: Two like poles (N-N or S-S) push apart, meaning they repel. Exam Tip: N-N or S-S -> repel.

fib.questionText: Unlike poles of a magnet ____ each other.
fib.explanation: Two unlike poles (N-S) pull together, meaning they attract. Exam Tip: N-S -> attract.

fib.questionText: The region around a magnet where its force can be felt is called the ____.
fib.explanation: The surrounding region where a magnet's force can be detected is called the magnetic field. Exam Tip: Shown using iron filings or a plotting compass.

fib.questionText: The process of making a material magnetic is called ____.
fib.explanation: Turning a material into a magnet is called magnetization. Exam Tip: Methods: stroking or using electric current.

fib.questionText: The process of removing magnetism from a magnet is called ____.
fib.explanation: Removing magnetism from a magnet is called demagnetization. Exam Tip: Heating, hammering or dropping demagnetizes a magnet.

fib.questionText: A temporary magnet formed by passing current through a coil around an iron core is called an ____.
fib.explanation: Current passed through a coil around an iron core creates a temporary magnet called an electromagnet. Exam Tip: Electromagnets work only while current flows.

fib.questionText: Materials such as iron, cobalt and nickel that are attracted to a magnet are called ____ materials.
fib.explanation: Iron, cobalt and nickel are examples of magnetic materials because they are attracted to a magnet. Exam Tip: Non-magnetic: wood, plastic, copper, aluminium.

fib.questionText: ____ iron is used for electromagnet cores because it magnetizes and demagnetizes quickly.
fib.explanation: Soft iron is used for electromagnet cores because it magnetizes and demagnetizes quickly. Exam Tip: Soft iron (temporary) vs steel (permanent).

fib.questionText: A freely suspended magnet will always come to rest pointing in the ____-south direction.
fib.explanation: A freely suspended magnet aligns with Earth's magnetic field, coming to rest pointing north-south. Exam Tip: This is the principle behind the magnetic compass.

tf.questionText: Like poles of two magnets repel each other.
tf.explanation: Two like poles, whether N-N or S-S, always push apart from each other. Exam Tip: N-N and S-S both repel.

tf.questionText: Unlike poles of two magnets repel each other.
tf.explanation: Unlike poles (N-S) pull towards each other; they attract rather than repel. Exam Tip: Unlike poles attract.

tf.questionText: Iron, cobalt and nickel are magnetic materials.
tf.explanation: These three metals (and their alloys) are strongly attracted to magnets, making them magnetic materials. Exam Tip: These three (and their alloys) are classic magnetic materials.

tf.questionText: Wood and plastic are magnetic materials.
tf.explanation: Wood and plastic are not attracted to magnets, so they are non-magnetic materials. Exam Tip: Only iron, cobalt, nickel (and alloys) are magnetic.

tf.questionText: An electromagnet is magnetic only while an electric current flows through its coil.
tf.explanation: Once the current is switched off, the soft iron core loses its magnetism almost immediately. Exam Tip: This on/off feature makes electromagnets useful in cranes and bells.

tf.questionText: Steel loses its magnetism very quickly, making it ideal for electromagnets.
tf.explanation: Steel retains its magnetism for a long time, which makes it suited to permanent magnets, not electromagnets. Exam Tip: Steel = permanent magnets; soft iron = electromagnets.

tf.questionText: Magnetic field lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole outside the magnet.
tf.explanation: Field lines travel from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet, forming closed loops. Exam Tip: Inside the magnet, lines continue from S back to N.

tf.questionText: Demagnetization can be caused by heating a magnet strongly or hammering it.
tf.explanation: Heat and mechanical shocks disturb the alignment of magnetic domains, removing magnetism. Exam Tip: Heat and mechanical shock disturb magnetic domains.

tf.questionText: A magnetic compass works because its needle aligns with the magnetic field of the Earth.
tf.explanation: The compass needle is a small magnet that turns to align with the Earth's magnetic field. Exam Tip: The compass needle points roughly north-south due to Earth's magnetic field.

tf.questionText: All materials in the world are attracted to a magnet.
tf.explanation: Only magnetic materials such as iron, cobalt, nickel and their alloys respond to a magnet's pull. Exam Tip: Only iron, cobalt, nickel (and alloys) respond to magnets.

summary.correctAnswer: A magnet is an object that attracts magnetic materials such as iron, cobalt and nickel; its ends, where the magnetic force is strongest, are called poles (north and south).
summary.explanation: The force of a magnet is weakest at its centre and strongest at its two poles. Exam Tip: Every magnet has both a north pole and a south pole - you cannot have one without the other.

summary.correctAnswer: Like poles (N-N or S-S) repel each other, while unlike poles (N-S) attract each other.
summary.explanation: This rule explains all the pushing and pulling behaviour observed between magnets. Exam Tip: Same letters repel, different letters attract.

summary.correctAnswer: The region around a magnet within which its magnetic force can be detected.
summary.explanation: It can be mapped using iron filings or a small plotting compass, showing field lines from north to south outside the magnet. Exam Tip: Field lines never cross and are closest together where the field is strongest.

summary.correctAnswer: Materials such as iron, cobalt and nickel (and their alloys) that are strongly attracted to a magnet.
summary.explanation: Materials like wood, plastic, copper and aluminium are non-magnetic and are not attracted. Exam Tip: Remember 'iron, cobalt, nickel' as the three classic magnetic elements.

summary.correctAnswer: The process of turning a magnetic material into a magnet, for example by stroking it with a magnet or passing an electric current through it.
summary.explanation: Magnetization aligns the tiny magnetic domains inside the material so they point in the same direction. Exam Tip: Common methods are the single-stroke (touch) method and the electrical method.

summary.correctAnswer: The process of removing magnetism from a magnet, caused by hammering, heating strongly, or dropping it repeatedly.
summary.explanation: These actions disturb the ordered alignment of magnetic domains, so the material loses its magnetism. Exam Tip: Careless storage or rough handling can accidentally demagnetize a magnet.

summary.correctAnswer: A temporary magnet produced by passing an electric current through a coil of wire wound around a soft iron core.
summary.explanation: An electromagnet is magnetic only while current flows through the coil, and loses its magnetism when the current is switched off. Exam Tip: Electromagnets are used in cranes, electric bells and relays because they can be switched on and off.

summary.correctAnswer: Hard magnetic materials, such as steel, keep their magnetism for a long time (used for permanent magnets); soft magnetic materials, such as soft iron, magnetize and demagnetize easily (used for electromagnets).
summary.explanation: Choosing the wrong material would make a permanent magnet fade quickly or an electromagnet fail to release its load. Exam Tip: Steel = hard/permanent; soft iron = soft/temporary.

summary.correctAnswer: A device with a freely suspended magnetized needle that aligns with the Earth's magnetic field to point north-south, used for direction-finding.
summary.explanation: Because the needle is a small magnet, it behaves exactly like a suspended bar magnet seeking the Earth's poles. Exam Tip: The north-seeking end of a compass needle points towards geographic north.

summary.correctAnswer: Magnets are used in devices such as compasses, electric bells, cranes, electric motors, generators and loudspeakers.
summary.explanation: These applications rely on either the permanent pull of a magnet or the switchable force of an electromagnet. Exam Tip: Link each use to whether it needs a permanent magnet or an electromagnet.

hoq.questionText: Two bar magnets, A and B, are brought close. A's north facing B's north pushes apart. A's north facing B's south pulls together. Explain using the law of magnetic poles.

options.text: Like poles (N-N) repel; unlike poles (N-S) attract - this matches the fundamental law of magnetism

hoq.explanation: N facing N is a like pole pairing - repel. N facing S is unlike - attract. Exam Tip: Same letters (N-N, S-S) -> repel; different letters (N-S) -> attract.

hoq.questionText: A technician needs an electromagnet on a crane to lift and release scrap iron. Explain why an electromagnet (not a permanent magnet) is correct, and what core to use.

options.text: A permanent magnet would work just as well
An electromagnet can be switched on to lift and off to release; a soft iron core should be used because it loses magnetism quickly when current stops
A steel core should be used because it keeps its magnetism

hoq.explanation: The crane needs to lift AND release - a permanent magnet could never let go. An electromagnet switches with current; soft iron demagnetizes quickly for clean release. Exam Tip: A steel core would be wrong - it keeps magnetism, so the iron would never drop.

hoq.questionText: A student wants to find whether an unlabelled metal bar is a magnet or plain iron, WITHOUT another magnet or compass. Describe a valid test.

options.text: Weigh the bar; magnets are always heavier

Bring one end of the bar near the CENTRE of an iron nail (not the ends) - if it attracts strongly there too and at the nail's ends, the bar is unmagnetized iron; if attraction is strong only near the bar's own ends and weak in the middle, it is a magnet
Heat the bar and see if it melts
There is no way to test this

hoq.explanation: A magnet's pull is strongest at its poles (ends) and weakest at its centre. Unmagnetized iron attracts fairly evenly along its length. Exam Tip: Test attraction at different points along the bar - concentrated at ends = magnet; even = plain iron.
